entities.name: Acacius of Beroea
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Acacius of Beroea (c. 322–c. 432) was a Syrian bishop who lived to approximately 110 years of age, becoming one of the longest-lived figures in early Church history and an eyewitness to nearly the entire period from the Council of Nicaea to the Council of Ephesus. Born in Syria and ordained by Eusebius of Samosata, he served as Bishop of Beroea (modern Aleppo) for over sixty years.

Acacius was a significant figure in the theological controversies of the fourth and fifth centuries, though his positions were often ambiguous or shifting. He participated in councils debating Arianism, was present at the Council of Antioch (379), the Council of Constantinople (381), and was active in the Nestorian controversy that culminated at Ephesus (431). His extremely long career made him a witness to virtually every major theological controversy of the era.

His relationship with John Chrysostom was complex: initially a patron of Chrysostom's cause, he eventually supported the synod that deposed him. His extreme longevity — reportedly dying at 110 — made him almost legendary in his own time, and his career documents the personal continuities that connected the Nicene age to the Nestorian controversies.
